## The three parameters of a sine signal

$$x(t) = A \sin(2 \pi f t + \phi)$$

- `A`: amplitude
- `f`: frequency, in Hz
- `T = 1 / f`: period, in s
- `omega = 2 pi f`: angular frequency, in rad/s
- `phi`: initial phase

actions.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fs = 100  # sample rate: 100 samples per second
duration = 1.0  # the signal lasts one second
t = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / fs)  # sample times from 0 to 1 second

clips.caption: First build the <c.aqua>sample time</c.aqua> axis: 100 <c.aqua>samples</c.aqua> per second, lasting one second.

actions.text:
A = 1.0  # amplitude A sets how tall the wave gets
f = 2.0  # frequency f sets cycles per second
phi = 0.0  # initial phase phi sets where the wave starts
x = A * np.sin(2 * np.pi * f * t + phi)  # sine formula: A·sin(2πft+φ)

clips.caption: Note this line carries the <c.aqua>amplitude</c.aqua> A, the <c.aqua>frequency</c.aqua> f and the <c.aqua>initial phase</c.aqua> phi at once.

actions.text:
print("samples:", t.size)
print("period (s):", 1 / f)
print("angular frequency (rad/s):", 2 * np.pi * f)

clips.caption: Finally print the <c.aqua>sample</c.aqua> count, the <c.aqua>period</c.aqua> and the <c.aqua>angular frequency</c.aqua>, then check each one after running.

First build a one-second <c.aqua>time axis</c.aqua>, then generate the sine from <c.aqua>amplitude</c.aqua>, <c.aqua>frequency</c.aqua> and initial phase. After running, check the sample count and the period.
We generate one second of data at 100 <c.aqua>samples</c.aqua> per second, so 100 time points. A is 1, f is 2 Hz, phi is 0. 2 Hz means two full cycles per second.
After running, confirm the <c.aqua>sample</c.aqua> count and the <c.aqua>period</c.aqua>. The period T is 1 over f, so 0.5 s here.
